aidb_assessment.novelty: High conceptual novelty within the paper’s framing: it connects next-task counterfactual valuation, compact repository/check anchors, on-policy memory-value estimation, and step-level provenance routing in one cost-aware framework. The strongest novelty is not generic memory compression but measuring value on the unseen next task from inherited state and using the same value notion for both memory design and actor adaptation.
aidb_assessment.rationale: The central comparisons are strong and unusually cost-aware; controlled component ablations and external checks add credibility. Confidence stops at medium because the principal evidence is author-run, concentrated in Python and one main benchmark/harness, some replay budgets are small, provenance is heuristic, and full reproducibility artifacts are unavailable in the supplied material.
aidb_assessment.usefulness: Potentially high for persistent coding agents where token and interaction costs matter. The frozen memory layer is immediately relevant because it reduces steps across six actors, while post-training shows larger gains for supported open-weight models. Adoption should wait for independent reproduction, multilingual and longer-history tests, latency measurements, and release of operational artifacts.

executive_summary: CoReMem targets agents solving successive tasks in a persistent repository, where memory is written before the next task is known. It prospectively values trajectory segments on the next task, retains compact location and executable-check anchors, and adapts the actor with an outcome-and-step reward plus provenance-gated memory-value credit. On ChainSWE, post-training improves resolution and efficiency across three open-weight actors; for the 27B actor, resolution rises from 21.0% to 25.7% while steps and total cache-aware tokens fall. Controlled ablations support the cost reward and gated credit, but evidence is concentrated in Python, one principal benchmark/harness, small model coverage, and author-run evaluations. Reproducibility is partial because detailed protocols are supplied but the code link is anonymous and several decisive artifacts are absent from the supplied blocks.

assumptions: Successive tasks share a repository state, and the next task is unknown when memory is written.
Repository locations and commands can be extracted reliably enough by string matching to serve as actionable and traceable anchors.
Paired stochastic rollouts from the same boundary provide a useful estimate of memory value despite sampling variance.
Steps and cache-aware tokens are adequate operational proxies for effort, although latency and energy are not measured.
The writer can produce a valid short structured memory, with a corrective retry or separate fallback call when needed.
key_components: Prospective segment valuation compares next-task runs from a fixed inherited state and estimates each segment’s contribution by removing it from the full trajectory memory.
The induced memory template preserves commands and repository content, compresses test output and changes, and drops reasoning narrative and scratch-file manifests.
Anchors are concrete repository locations or executable checks that the next task can use directly and that also enable traceable attribution.
Training groups contain no-memory sessions, own-memory sessions, and one misplaced-memory session to discourage indiscriminate memory following.
The reward prioritizes successful resolution over all step savings, then penalizes step count within successful sessions and credits partial test progress for failures.
Provenance-gated credit applies the measured memory-value term to memory-driven steps while retaining session-outcome credit on every step.
method.overview: CoReMem first estimates prospective memory value by rerunning the unseen next task from the same inherited repository state with and without candidate memory. It partitions the prior trajectory by role, ablates segments, and converts useful material into compact anchors: repository locations and executable checks. It then post-trains the actor in rollout groups mixing own memory, no memory, and memory from another repository. A reward ranks every successful run above failures while charging steps within successful runs. The mean own-memory versus no-memory reward gap estimates on-policy memory value; that extra value is assigned only to steps whose first-use anchors can be traced to memory, while all steps retain outcome credit.

open_questions: Can the memory template and provenance matcher transfer to statically typed, compiled, polyglot, or non-test-centric repositories?
What is the separate causal contribution of general post-training versus memory-conditioned training when both are evaluated with and without memory under matched checkpoints?
How should multiple memories be merged, invalidated, refreshed, access-controlled, and redacted over long task chains?
Do step and token reductions translate into lower wall-clock latency, energy, and monetary cost under realistic parallel tool execution and cache policies?
Would semantic or execution-level provenance outperform anchor string matching without introducing excessive training cost?
How sensitive are results to writer quality, memory corruption, repository drift, and adversarial or stale commands?

problem.importance: Existing memory systems may improve resolution while increasing overall cost: the paper reports that none of the tested existing forms reduced both steps and total tokens, and each spent more memory-module tokens than it saved.
problem.scope: The work studies sequential coding sessions in a persistent workspace. Each next task inherits earlier edits, while only a memory text—not the preceding trajectory—crosses the session boundary.
problem.statement: An agent must decide what information to preserve after one coding task for an unknown later task on the inherited repository, and must learn when using that information reduces work rather than distracting execution.

proposed_experiments.baseline: A factorial comparison using the same base actor and training budget: untrained/no memory, untrained/CoReMem, post-trained/no memory, and post-trained/CoReMem, plus a post-trained shuffled-memory arm.
proposed_experiments.hypothesis: CoReMem’s post-training benefit is specifically larger when valid cross-task memory is present than when no memory is present, beyond general efficient-coding adaptation.
proposed_experiments.primary_metric: Difference-in-differences for resolve per total cache-aware token, with paired repository-chain confidence intervals; also report resolution and steps separately.
proposed_experiments.stop_condition: Stop after the preregistered number of independent repository chains and replays; reject the memory-specific hypothesis if the interaction confidence interval includes zero or if resolution decreases.

proposed_experiments.baseline: Matched training runs with identical initialization, rollouts, reward, and compute, differing only between gated credit, whole-trajectory credit, and outcome-only credit.
proposed_experiments.hypothesis: Provenance-gated credit improves selective memory use more reliably than whole-trajectory credit across model sizes and languages.
proposed_experiments.primary_metric: Misplaced-memory step cost jointly with valid-memory resolution benefit, evaluated on held-out repositories in at least one non-Python language.
proposed_experiments.stop_condition: Stop after fixed seeds and replay budgets; reject the hypothesis if gating fails to reduce misplaced-memory cost without reducing valid-memory resolution benefit on most preregistered model-language settings.

proposed_experiments.baseline: Latest-memory-only, unbounded concatenation, fixed-size recency selection, and CoReMem with explicit merge/refresh/invalidation over long task chains.
proposed_experiments.hypothesis: A bounded refresh policy preserves CoReMem’s efficiency over long repository histories better than retaining only the latest memory or concatenating all memories.
proposed_experiments.primary_metric: Resolve per total token across chain position, accompanied by wall-clock latency and stale-anchor execution rate.
proposed_experiments.stop_condition: Stop at the preregistered chain length or when all methods exceed the same memory budget; reject the hypothesis if refreshed CoReMem does not improve area under the resolve-per-token-by-position curve or increases stale-anchor use.

results.context: This is the strongest central comparison because it jointly improves task success and both reported effort measures. It compares the post-trained actor plus CoReMem against the same actor family without memory on the held-out test split.
results.result: For Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 on ChainSWE, CoReMem raises overall resolve rate from 21.0% without memory to 25.7%, while mean steps fall from 35.1 to 29.2 and total cache-aware tokens per session fall from 32.2K to 28.5K.

results.context: This aggregate supports cross-model consistency within the tested open-weight set, but it does not cover the three API-served actors because they were evaluated only with the frozen memory layer.
